strengths: Novel reinterpretation of F2SA as finite difference approximation to hyper-gradient enables natural extension to higher-order methods
Solid theoretical analysis with both upper bounds (O(pκ^{9+2/p}ϵ^{-4-2/p})) and lower bounds (Ω(ϵ^{-4}))
Cleaner lower bound construction using fully separable problem formulation, avoiding technical issues in prior work
Improves prior complexity from κ^12ϵ^{-6} to κ^11ϵ^{-6} for first-order smooth case
Rigorous high-dimensional Faà di Bruno formula analysis providing tighter bounds than prior work
Fully first-order methods are more practical and scalable than HVP-based approaches
weaknesses: Substantial gap between upper and lower bounds unresolved: O(ϵ^{-6}) upper vs Ω(ϵ^{-4}) lower for p=1, a factor of ϵ^{-2} gap
Minimal experimental validation: only one simple benchmark (20 Newsgroup), no systematic study of varying p, observation that p=2 is optimal lacks theoretical explanation
High-order smoothness assumption (Assumption 2.5) is restrictive; practical scenarios requiring p≥3 are unclear or absent
Large condition number dependence κ^{9+2/p} remains problematic (κ^11 for p=1, no improvement over prior F2SA bound of κ^12); acknowledged as open problem
Near-optimality requires p=Ω(log κ/ϵ/log log κ/ϵ), which can be impractically large, limiting practical applicability
Incremental algorithmic novelty: straightforward extension of F2SA double-loop structure, main change is hyper-gradient estimator
Normalized gradient step (Remark 3.2) used for analytical convenience but unclear if necessary; potential practical performance impact
Missing concrete applications and problem characterization satisfying high-order smoothness assumptions beyond theoretical discussion

strengths: Novel interpretation connecting bilevel optimization to finite difference approximations, naturally motivating algorithmic extensions
Solid theoretical improvements: O(κ¹¹ϵ⁻⁶) for p=1 (vs prior O(κ¹²ϵ⁻⁶)) and O(κ⁹ϵ⁻⁵) for p=2; generalizable to arbitrary p
Matching upper Ω(ϵ⁻⁴) and lower Ω(ϵ⁻⁴) bounds in high-smoothness regime (p=Ω(log ϵ⁻¹/log log ϵ⁻¹)), demonstrating near-optimality
Technically rigorous proofs using high-dimensional Faa di Bruno formula and careful finite difference analysis
Practical algorithm F2SA-2 maintains O(1) lower-level problems per iteration while improving complexity
Comprehensive appendices with full proofs and additional experimental results
weaknesses: Assumption 2.5 (high-order smoothness in y) is highly restrictive; only verified for logistic regression; becomes increasingly unrealistic for p≥3
Unresolved condition number gap of Ω(κ⁹) between upper bound κ^(9+2/p) and lower bound (for constant κ); recent concurrent work shows tighter O(κ^(5/2)) and O(κ⁴) lower bounds
Significant gap between upper/lower bounds for practical smoothness orders (p=1,2,3); matching regime p=Ω(log ϵ⁻¹/log log ϵ⁻¹) is impractical (e.g., p≈20 for ϵ=10⁻⁶)
Weak experimental validation: only two settings tested, no ablations on smoothness order p, MLP experiments violate smoothness assumptions, missing comparisons to recent methods
Limited algorithmic novelty: once finite difference connection established, extension is straightforward; main contribution is theoretical analysis
Remark 3.1 suggests normalized gradient step may be unnecessary but claim is not fully substantiated with analysis for standard gradient descent
Practical applicability unclear: no guidance on when to use F2SA-p over F2SA, hidden constants in Assumption 2.5 not explicitly bounded
